speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) what are the Ministry’s plans to improve footpath safety back to levels before PMDs were allowed on footpaths; and (b) what is the estimated timeframe that the Ministry has set to achieve this objective.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In February 2017, we debated at length in this House and passed the Active Mobility Bill to regulate the use of active mobility devices (AMDs) on public paths and to support active mobility.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Prior to this, motorised personal mobility devices (PMDs) were not allowed on footpaths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: There are more than 5,500 kilometres (km) of footpaths islandwide, almost double the 3,500 km of roads.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The convenience of being able to use these devices on footpaths for first-and-last-mile commutes, as well as for food delivery services, contributed to their popularity and a sharp increase in their population to close to 100,000 today.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Over the last two years, we have put in great efforts to promote the safe use of motorised PMDs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We legislated compliance standards for the devices and their proper usage.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Working closely with the Active Mobility Advisory Panel (AMAP), we introduced a Safe Riding Programme and reduced speed limits on footpaths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We stepped up enforcement and, through the MyTransport.SG mobile application, obtained regular public feedback on errant users and hotspots.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Despite significant efforts, we continue to encounter errant riders who use non-compliant devices and ride dangerously.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We catch an average of about 370 offenders per month.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The number of accidents involving motorised PMDs continues to rise.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: There have been more severe accidents and even a fatal one involving a cyclist in September.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Many riders have themselves suffered severe injuries, including a few who lost their lives.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Singaporeans and several Members of Parliament have called for harsher measures against errant riders.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Others have demanded that motorised PMDs be fitted with tamper-proof global positioning system (GPS) trackers.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Unfortunately, this will affect their circuitry, making them non-compliant to the UL2272 standard.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As more accidents occur, the calls for a total ban on PMD usage get louder.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are not alone in having to revisit existing rules governing the use of motorised PMDs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Last week, France announced that it would no longer allow the riding of e-scooters on its pavements.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This followed hundreds of e-scooter-related incidents, including several deaths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Cities have allowed the use of such devices on footpaths as they are non-pollutive, inexpensive and, if properly used, convenient for short intra-town travels.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We expected the co-sharing of footpaths to be challenging but were hopeful that, with public education, PMD users would be gracious and responsible.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To allow time for users to adjust, we will provide an advisory period until 31 December 2019.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This ban from footpaths will not apply to those with mobility challenges who ride personal mobility aids like motorised wheelchairs and mobility scooters.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The ban will also not apply to bicycles.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are aware that the banning of e-scooter usage on footpaths will impact food delivery riders who rely on them for work.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We understand from the major food delivery companies that their deliveries are largely done by motorcycles and delivery vehicles.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Less than 30% of Deliveroo and FoodPanda's riders use e-scooters.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Land Transport Authority (LTA) will work with the food delivery companies to allow as many of their delivery riders to switch to motorcycles or bicycles.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This move is not a complete ban of e-scooters in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue to allow them on dedicated cycling paths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are stepping up the construction of such cycling paths to provide clear separation between pedestrians and e-scooters, as in Ang Mo Kio and Tampines Town.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA will be adding dedicated cycling paths in towns, such as Woodlands, Toa Payoh and Choa Chu Kang.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As for the fire safety concerns, we have brought forward the deadline for compliance with the UL2272 standard to 1 July next year.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will also be introducing a regular inspection regime to ensure compliance.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Of the remaining 20%, those which fail our inspection regime will likewise not be allowed to be used on public paths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This will effectively reduce the population of e-scooters on public paths significantly.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are offering owners of non-compliant e-scooters an incentive of $100 if they dispose of their non-compliant devices early.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since the rollout of the scheme on 23 September 2019 to 31 October 2019, more than 4,800 e-scooters have been disposed.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have decided to extend the early disposal incentive scheme from 30 November to 31 December 2019.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We strongly urge the owners of non-compliant e-scooters to dispose of their devices early to protect themselves and their neighbours from unnecessary fire risks.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Members asked about the sale of non-UL2272 certified devices.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since 1 July 2019, it has been an offence for retailers to display, advertise or sell non-UL2272 certified PMDs for use on public paths in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Those convicted may be liable to a fine of up to $5,000 and/or jail of up to three months for the first offence.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We hope to have Members’ understanding and support for this new policy.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Speaker, I want to thank the Senior Minister of State for making the announcement.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I think many people will welcome that ban on shared footpaths.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But the Senior Minister of State has not answered my question because an announcement that a ban will take place would still need to be enforced.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, may I ask whether the Ministry will consider increasing the number of enforcement teams, so that we can actively enforce the rules, especially now that the rules are that you are going to ban these PMDs on the shared footpaths?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Will the Ministry of Transport (MOT) do that and by how many?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Because now that you are going to ban the use of PMDs on shared footpaths, I would expect that your enforcement should be stepped up.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In addition to AMEOs, we are also forming more Active Mobility Patrol teams within the community.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will be working with the various constituencies to form as many Active Mobility Patrol teams as possible so that they can also help in the public education of PMD users.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At the same time, we also have what we call "Blue-Rangers" who are LTA officers who volunteer to take up the added responsibility of going around to educate PMD users on the various rules and regulations, as well as to remind them that from tomorrow onwards, it will be illegal to ride PMDs on footpaths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Speaker, may I ask the Senior Minister of State in respect of part (c) of my Question No 8 "whether the Government will consider mandatory safe-riding certification courses with disqualification rights"?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In respect of the calls for age limit both by the Active Mobility Panel as well as in my previous Parliamentary Question, will the Government consider an age limit for riders riding PMDs?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also be grateful if the Senior Minister of State can answer Question No 11.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With regard to his question on whether there should be any mandatory safe-riding certification courses, I would like to share with the House that AMAP has recently submitted their recommendations on certain aspects of active mobility and one of which includes a mandatory theory test, which is slightly different from the safe-riding certification.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But that may be a good step forward because by having a mandatory theory test, this will remind them of some of the various new rules and regulations on PMD usage, as well as some of the safety measures that they should adopt when using PMDs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We do not think that a safe-riding certification course will be necessary at this point in time because riding a PMD is very different from operating a motorcycle or, for that matter, a motor vehicle.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It is actually much easier to do so.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The question is whether the PMD user will exercise their due diligence and responsibility in riding the device in a safe manner.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As to the age limit, similarly, AMAP has also recommended that the age limit be brought down to 16.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At the same time, we are also moving upstream to look at how we can impose an import control of such non-compliant PMDs, so that we do not see such non-complaint PMDs being marketed in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are working together with the necessary Government agencies to see how we can go about doing that.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The first question is that the Senior Minister of State mentioned that 12 retailers were caught for flouting the rules.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Of these 12 retailers, how many are physical retailers and how many are online retailers?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The second question is: how does LTA or MOT detect those retailers that are flouting the rules?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For the physical retailers, it will be easier.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But for the online retailers, it may be more difficult.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Some of the online retailers may also be reselling their used PMDs which are non-compliant with the UL2272 standard on some of the platforms.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The third question is that the Senior Minister of State mentioned that by the end of the year, it will increase the enforcement team to 200 people.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I think Mr Ang will agree with me that it is very difficult to control or even prosecute online retailers because many of them are actually located outside Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But having said that, LTA works very closely with some of the major online retailers, for example, Lazada, to request that they put on the website some of the rules and regulations of PMD usage in Singapore, especially with respect to the device criteria allowed for sale in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: On the Member's third question on the number of AMEOs, like I have mentioned, we will increase to 200.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Offhand I do not have the exact number of AMEOs that we have right now, but I think it is in the region of 100-plus.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One, I would like to ask whether there will be any upgrading of the path in Nee Soon Town because the cycling path and the footpath side by side, they are the same colour, so whatever that you ban, I do not see that it will make any difference in Nee Soon Town.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Two, despite the ban on footpaths, will the Ministry consider mandatory licensing for PMD riders as well as insurance?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Because as you beef up the infrastructure, as we go along, the number will increase again.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Three, on the registration number on PMDs, as I had mentioned in my question last month, it is too small and it is not visible at all at night.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will this part be looked into and reviewed?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Four, will the Ministry consider making speed limit installation compulsory moving forward for new PMDs?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Last but not least, it is a good move, but the next matter that the residents will be afraid of is bicycles.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We do not have any registration numbers on the bicycles.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, when it comes to accidents, there is no way that they can identify the cyclist.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The very first is on upgrading the paths in Nee Soon South.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In fact, we will be upgrading the paths in all the different towns in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Of course, we will be focusing on those where the use of active mobility is the highest and then we will try to do so for the rest of the towns as soon as possible.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: If there are any particular paths or areas where Er Dr Lee Bee Wah is concerned about, we can always look at it and see how we can tap on the funding that I have announced during the Ministerial Statement on improving certain hotspot areas, so that the risk of conflict can be minimised in those areas.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But we already have various regimes in place, such as the mandatory registration of PMD device itself.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are also currently actively studying some of the recommendations put up by AMAP, one of which is the mandatory theory test.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Like I have explained to Mr Dennis Tan, the intent is to inculcate safe riding habits amongst PMD users and, at the same time, also to remind PMD users of some of the rules and regulations that are in place.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As to whether we should have mandatory third-party liability insurance, we have been actively studying this issue.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are also working with the insurance companies to see how we can bring down the price of the premium for such a product.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At the same time, we also encourage all PMD users to consider purchasing third-party liability insurance because it provides the necessary protection and peace of mind.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We also take back the Member's suggestion on the registration label for registered PMDs and we can work with LTA to see how we can make the font size more readable and easier to identify.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With the implementation of the prohibition of e-scooter use on footpaths from tomorrow, there is no longer a need to limit these devices to 10 km/h.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At the same time, if there are any illegal modifications of the speed limit of the PMDs, LTA will come down hard on these PMD users who illegally modify their devices.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As to bicycle registration, we have debated on this topic many years back in Parliament whether we should register cyclists.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The decision then was not to because it will actually impede the take-up of active mobility, especially bicycles.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At this point in time, many members of the public are supportive of the use of bicycles in their town as well as amongst the neighbourhood.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The main concern now is that of PMD usage, especially those who are reckless and riding them dangerously.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will focus on the control of PMD use.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The recent announcement on the ban on footpaths will be the right step forward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Senior Minister of State consider extending an incentive for the disposal of compliant PMDs?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I am asking this because although this decision will greatly improve pedestrian safety, it will also harm the value of all PMDs, even compliant ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And if you get people to turn them in if they have no longer a use for them, it will reduce the risks of one using it and address any harm suffered by responsible owners of these PMDs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I understand where the Member is coming from.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The reason why we are doing so is because of the risk of fire and, therefore, we will not be extending this incentive to PMDs that are compliant because, for PMDs that are compliant, they can still continue to use them on the cycling paths as well as the PCNs and we are not totally restricting its use altogether.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With the ban of using PMDs in void decks, this measure would largely address the safety concerns of residents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also think that this represents an openness and willingness on the part of MOT to revisit issues when the circumstances warrant it and I think Members of this House should acknowledge that.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is also a matter of regret because the first decision to rely on the conduct of PMD users by self-regulating appears to be an experiment which somehow failed, but it is not a wrong decision in itself.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My supplementary question is in relation to enforcement in Pedestrian-only Zones (POZs).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I hear the hon Senior Minister of State, we have enforcement officers under the Active Mobility Act.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: When we first started debating on this topic in 2017, the collective decision then was to allow the use of PMDs on footpaths with the necessary mitigating measures in place, which we have done very thoroughly over the past two years.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But at the same time, we understand that we should not push for connectivity at all costs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Public safety is still paramount and, looking at the current situation, it is not possible for the Government not to make a decisive decision.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Therefore, the decision to prohibit the use of PMDs on footpaths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As to the POZs, with this current announcement, we will be going back to the five pilot sites at the various Town Councils to work with the advisers to see whether they would like to proceed with the implementation of POZs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Because with the current ban of PMDs on footpaths, the danger posed by PMDs in such areas will be significantly reduced.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Therefore, the question is whether we should continue with the POZs to prohibit the use of bicycles in these town centres.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For those advisers who still want to continue with the implementation of POZs, LTA, together with MOT, will work very closely with the adviser to implement the POZs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With regard to enforcement, we should adopt the attitude that we are in this together.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Town Council officers, together with the LTA enforcement officers, will try to make it as safe as possible for the pedestrians at the POZs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am rising to follow up on a question I raised to the Senior Minister of State on enforcement of PMD bans at void decks with respect to Town Councils.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Aljunied-Hougang Town Council (AHTC) took a position previously, but in light of the Minister's announcement, we will align our rules to the Government's stand on the matter.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State how he sees this decision affecting the food delivery businesses and, more importantly, the PMD riders who are dependent on the PMDs to earn a living and whether there will be existing measures to help them to continue to have a way to do their business.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I must say that we share the same concern when deliberating on this measure.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have been engaging the three major food delivery companies – Food Panda, Grab Food as well as Deliveroo.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For Food Panda, only about 12% of their food deliveries are done by PMDs, Deliveroo about 5%.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We do not have the exact statistics from Grab Food.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are encouraging the food delivery companies and are working with them to see how we can convert as many of these PMD delivery personnel to either use motorcycles or bicycles because we do see that some of the companies do use bicycles for food delivery as well.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, Food Panda has about 16% of their food deliveries done on bicycles.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand from the Senior Minister of State that it will be challenging certainly to have an enforcement team to enforce this on the ground.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Government consider perhaps using technology and enhanced technology in this area?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, with a sufficient closed-circuit television (CCTV) or camera network and perhaps more advanced recognition technology, would this be possible in the future to use such technology to identify those who break the law?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Again, similar technology has been used in the enforcement of traffic regulations or even illegal parking along double yellow lines, for example.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The short answer is yes, we will see how we can use technology to strengthen our enforcement capabilities.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In fact, in previous Parliamentary Sittings, I had already shared that LTA is currently piloting the use of CCTVs for that purpose.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At the same time, we have also implemented MyTransport.SG where the public can snap a picture of the errant rider and, if possible, try to identify the errant rider.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: If not, at least it will provide some information on where the possible hotspots are.
